```python
out, _ = workflow_ops.set_widget(wf, graph, 14, "seed", 999)
```

Result:

```
before: ["Seedance 2.0", "a pirate dances", "720p", "16:9", 5, true, true, 118383194, "randomize", false]
after:  ["Seedance 2.0", "a pirate dances", "720p", "16:9", 5, true, true, 118383194,          999, false]
                                                                          ^^^^^^^^^  ^^^
                                                                          seed       control marker
                                                                          unchanged  clobbered
```

The user asked to set the seed. The seed is untouched at index 7, and the `control_after_generate` marker at index 8 became `999`.

## Cause

`Graph.widget_order_for_node` expands a dynamic combo's selected option using the **current** catalog, so it produces eleven slots for this ten-value save:

```
slot 0: model
slot 1: model.prompt
slot 2: model.resolution
slot 3: model.ratio
slot 4: model.duration
slot 5: model.generate_audio
slot 6: model.auto_downscale
slot 7: model.auto_upscale   <-- the save never had this widget
slot 8: seed                 <-- but the file's seed is at index 7
slot 9: control_after_generate
slot 10: watermark
```

`_expand_widget_entries` (`comfy_cli/cql/engine.py:4550`) walks declared ports and, at a dynamic combo, inlines the selected option's sub-inputs from `_dynamic_combo_sub_ports`. That list is today's option layout. The save's layout is recorded on the node, in its `inputs[].widget` markers, and nothing reads them: every slot from the inserted sub-input onward is off by one.

The docstring at `:4563-4565` says one walk serves both the static catalog and "the value-aware order `set-widget` indexes by", which is true and is exactly why both are wrong together here.

## Why it is quiet

Nothing detects it. `widgets_values` stays the same length, the written value is type-valid for *some* slot, and the node still converts and runs. The user sees their seed unchanged and may simply retry. The corrupted `control_after_generate` surfaces later as a validation error naming a field the user never touched, or as a seed that will not randomize.

## Relationship to the conversion fix

#1069 makes the **convert** path expand these sub-inputs in the order the save records, which is what the frontend does. That fixes reading. It does not change this, because `set-widget` resolves its index through `widget_order_for_node` instead.

Worth being precise about the direction, because it is easy to read this as a regression introduced by that PR: the edit path was already writing the wrong slot for such a save, and both paths were wrong together before. #1069 fixes one of them, which makes the other one visible. The two now disagree, and the edit side is the one that is wrong.

## Suggested fix

Give `_expand_widget_entries` the same saved-order input the converter now uses: when the node records `inputs[].widget` markers, order the selected option's sub-inputs by those markers and omit any the save does not name, falling back to the catalog order when the node records none. That is the same rule and the same evidence as `_saved_sub_order` in #1069, so the right shape is probably one shared helper both call rather than two implementations of it. Tracked as part of the shared-resolution work in #1077.

### Task Decomposition

| ID | Sub-task | Tier | Est | Depends | Acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Regression test first: `set-widget seed` on the save above must change index 7 and leave index 8 as `"randomize"` | routine | 20m | — | Test is red on `main` |
| 2 | Extract the saved-sub-order rule from #1069 into one helper both the converter and `_expand_widget_entries` call | analytical | 45m | #1069 landing | No duplicated rule; both call sites covered by its own tests |
| 3 | Thread the node (not just `widgets_values`) into `widget_order_for_node` / `_expand_widget_entries` | analytical | 45m | 2 | Signature change absorbed by callers: `set-widget`, `slots`, `validate`, `add_node` |
| 4 | Audit the other consumers of that order for the same off-by-one: `editable_widget_names`, `workflow slots`, `validate` | analytical | 30m | 3 | Each either correct or covered by a test |
| 5 | Check whether a `control_after_generate` slot already corrupted by this is repairable on read | routine | 30m | 1 | A documented answer; a repair only if it is unambiguous |

Task 1 stands alone and is worth landing even if the rest waits, because it pins the bug.

Found while closing out #1069, where I had told a reviewer this would be filed separately.

issues.title: bug: WorkBuddy and OpenCode report a missing Scope as a version mismatch
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

WorkBuddy and OpenCode report every HTTP 404 as `version_mismatch`. The Server returns 404 in two cases:

- A route that does not exist returns an uncoded 404, `{"detail":"Not Found"}`. Only this case means that the plugin and the Server versions do not match.
- A configured Scope that does not exist returns a coded 404, `{"error":{"code":"scope_not_found",...}}`. The Server returns it from `POST /v1/scope-bindings/resolve`, and also from `/v1/context/prepare`, `/v1/sources/content`, and `/v1/memory/flush` when the request names an unknown `scope_id`.

For a coded 404, the version-mismatch advice is wrong. The documented action for `version_mismatch` is to install the package and plugin from the same ref (for example, [`troubleshoot.md:402`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/docs/en/docs/operate/troubleshoot.md#L402)), and that does not help when the Scope itself is missing. The plugin contract also says that `version_mismatch` "MUST NOT be inferred from a direct resource lookup" ([`plugin-contract.md:34`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/docs/en/development/plugin-contract.md#L34)).

Where the mapping happens (master `0c1dfc28`):

- **WorkBuddy hook.** [`workbuddy_powercontext_hook.py:202`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/workbuddy/plugins/powercontext/hooks/workbuddy_powercontext_hook.py#L202) maps a Scope resolution 404 to `version_mismatch`, and [`:552-553`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/workbuddy/plugins/powercontext/hooks/workbuddy_powercontext_hook.py#L552-L553) does the same for a prepare 404. The error code is lost before either mapping runs. `ScopeBindingStatusError` ([`scripts/workspace_scope.py:65-71`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/workbuddy/plugins/powercontext/scripts/workspace_scope.py#L65-L71), raised at [`:262`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/workbuddy/plugins/powercontext/scripts/workspace_scope.py#L262)) and `_HttpStatusError` ([hook `:99-102`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/workbuddy/plugins/powercontext/hooks/workbuddy_powercontext_hook.py#L99-L102), raised at [`:490`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/workbuddy/plugins/powercontext/hooks/workbuddy_powercontext_hook.py#L490)) keep only the status and never read the error body.
- **OpenCode statusline.** [`src/tui.tsx:152-157`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/opencode/plugins/powercontext/src/tui.tsx#L152-L157) returns `version_mismatch` for any 404 and shows "PC version mismatch". This mapping applies to Scope resolution (`scopeFailureOutcome`) and to `get_stats` (`statsFailureOutcome`). The code is already available: `ServerResponseError.code` ([`src/errors.ts:55-66`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/opencode/plugins/powercontext/src/errors.ts#L55-L66)) holds `error.code` from the body, but `httpOutcome` reads only the status. In the `get_stats` path, [`src/invoke.ts:74`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/opencode/plugins/powercontext/src/invoke.ts#L74) gives an uncoded 404 the fallback code `not_found`, so `ToolResult.code` alone cannot tell the two cases apart.

The other hosts already classify a 404 by its error code. Pi, OpenClaw, DSH, and Hermes report `version_mismatch` only for an uncoded 404 from a compatibility or availability path (`isVersionMismatch` / `COMPATIBILITY_OR_AVAILABILITY_PATHS`). Kimi Code and ZCode map 404 to `not_found`, never to `version_mismatch`. Claude Code and Codex treat a 404 from Scope resolution the same way, and #2317 fixes that.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Start a Server from master with the default settings (loopback, authentication off).
2. Set a Scope ID that does not exist: `POWERCONTEXT_WORKBUDDY_SCOPE_ID=scp_missing` for WorkBuddy, or `POWERCONTEXT_OPENCODE_SCOPE_ID=scp_missing` for OpenCode.
3. WorkBuddy: submit a prompt. OpenCode: open the TUI and look at the statusline.

To see the two response shapes directly (with authentication on, add the `Authorization` header to both requests):

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/scope-bindings/resolve -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"explicit_scope_id":"scp_missing"}'
# 404 {"error":{"code":"scope_not_found","message":"The requested Scope was not found.","details":null}}
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/no-such-route
# 404 {"detail":"Not Found"}
```

### Expected behavior

Only a 404 without an error code is reported as `version_mismatch`. A coded 404 such as `scope_not_found` is reported as `invalid_response` and carries its status and code, the same classification that #2317 applies to Claude Code and Codex.

### Actual behavior

Observed with both hosts' master code against a master Server:

- WorkBuddy writes `{"component":"powercontext.workbuddy.recall","event":"context_prepare","outcome":"version_mismatch","http_status":404}` to stderr.
- The OpenCode statusline shows "PC version mismatch".

### Proposed fix

Classify a 404 by its error code, as #2317 does. Do not change the Server.

- **WorkBuddy.** Read `error.code` from the body of an error response in both `workspace_scope.py` and `_post_json`, and keep it on `ScopeBindingStatusError` and `_HttpStatusError`. Map only a 404 without a code to `version_mismatch`; any other 404 becomes `invalid_response`. Add `error_code` to the diagnostic event when the code is present. A code is not content, so the event stays content-free.
- **OpenCode.** Pass the error code into `httpOutcome`, using `ServerResponseError.code` for Scope resolution. For `get_stats`, carry the Server's code separately from the `not_found` fallback, or check `error.code` before `errorResult` rewrites it.
- **Docs and tests.** Update the WorkBuddy failure table in both locales ([`workbuddy.md:291`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/docs/en/docs/integrations/workbuddy.md#L291)). The OpenCode test [`tests/tui.spec.tsx:265`](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/0c1dfc289b28e9f529555fb57bf771ce51103913/integrations/opencode/plugins/powercontext/tests/tui.spec.tsx#L265) currently expects "PC version mismatch" for a coded 404 (`{"error":{"code":"failure"}}`), so it has to change. Add a test for a coded 404 and for an uncoded 404 in each host.

In step 4 of #2250, WorkBuddy moves onto the Python lifecycle module and OpenCode onto the TypeScript one. That plan does not allow a move to change behavior, so this fix lands before the move, as #2317 does for Claude Code and Codex.

### Environment

- PowerContext version: master `0c1dfc28`
- Hosts: WorkBuddy, OpenCode

Related: #2317 (the same fix for Claude Code and Codex), #2250 (lifecycle plan).

### Are you willing to submit a PR to fix this bug?

- [x] Yes, I would like to submit a PR.

issues.title: Event-based continuous-energy run in openmc.lib segfaults after a multigroup run in the same process
issues.body:
## Bug Description

When a multigroup model and then a continuous-energy model are run one after the other in one Python process through `openmc.lib` (`Model.init_lib()`, `openmc.lib.run()`, `Model.finalize_lib()`), both event-based, the process is killed by a segmentation fault during the continuous-energy run. In the runs that showed OpenMC's output, the last line printed was that run's `K EIGENVALUE SIMULATION` header, before any batch line. The same pair of runs completes when both are history-based, and in event-based mode the other orders complete: continuous energy then multigroup, multigroup twice, and continuous energy twice.

Measured with the script below, which runs each order and mode in its own child process, on develop at aa4afc41e and at 3aec0edef (the same output on both):

- multigroup then continuous energy, event-based: the child is killed by signal 11 (SIGSEGV) after the multigroup run completes;
- the same pair, history-based: both runs complete, with k-eff 0.74824 and 1.78385;
- the other three orders, in both modes: every run completes, with the same k-eff for each model.

A second script, with other models, gives the same result on develop aa4afc41e: the event-based continuous-energy run after a multigroup run crashes, and the history-based one completes. We found this while writing tests that run several models through `openmc.lib` in one pytest process (#4199); those tests run their in-process models in history mode for this reason.

Expected: the continuous-energy run completes, as it does history-based or as the first run of a process.

**Reading of the code, not tested.** Line numbers are at aa4afc41e; the C++ sources are the same on the current develop (3aec0edef).

- In event-based mode, `openmc_simulation_init()` sets up the particle buffer with `init_event_queues()` (`src/simulation.cpp:104-107`), which calls `simulation::particles.resize(n_particles)` (`src/event.cpp:40`). `resize()` keeps the `Particle` objects already in the vector.
- A `Particle` sizes its cross-section cache when it is constructed: `neutron_xs_.resize(data::nuclides.size())` (`src/particle_data.cpp:109`). In a multigroup run, `data::nuclides` is empty.
- `openmc_finalize()` sets `settings::event_based = false` (`src/finalize.cpp:98`) before it calls `free_memory()` (`src/finalize.cpp:199`), and `free_memory()` clears the buffer only `if (settings::event_based)` (`src/finalize.cpp:64-66`, through `free_event_queues()`, `src/event.cpp:51`).
- If so, the buffer survives `openmc_finalize()`, and the continuous-energy run reuses particles whose `neutron_xs_` is empty, which `neutron_xs(i)` (`include/openmc/particle_data.h:587`) indexes without a check. This would fit the orders that complete: a multigroup run does not use `neutron_xs_`, two runs of the same model have the same number of nuclides, and history-based transport constructs one `Particle` per thread each time it transports a batch (`src/simulation.cpp:969-971`).

No debugger was attached and no change was tried, so this is a reading, not a diagnosis.

Not tried: MPI builds; thread counts other than 2; fixed-source mode; continuous-energy models other than these two, or other nuclear data libraries; released versions.

## Steps to Reproduce

The multigroup half needs no nuclear data: the script writes a one-group library. The continuous-energy half needs `OPENMC_CROSS_SECTIONS` pointing to a library with H1 and U235. Run it in an empty directory:

```python
"""Run a multigroup (mg) and a continuous-energy (ce) model one after the
other through openmc.lib in one process, in event-based or history-based
mode. Each order and mode runs in its own child process; the driver prints
the child's return code (negative = killed by a signal, -11 = SIGSEGV).
The ce model needs OPENMC_CROSS_SECTIONS with H1 and U235."""
import os, sys, subprocess, json
from pathlib import Path

def mg_model(d):
    import openmc
    groups = openmc.mgxs.EnergyGroups([0.0, 20.0e6])
    xs = openmc.XSdata('fuel', groups); xs.order = 0
    xs.set_total([1.0]); xs.set_absorption([0.5]); xs.set_fission([0.15])
    xs.set_nu_fission([0.375]); xs.set_scatter_matrix([[[0.5]]]); xs.set_chi([1.0])
    lib = openmc.MGXSLibrary(groups); lib.add_xsdata(xs); lib.export_to_hdf5(d / 'mg.h5')
    m = openmc.Material(); m.set_density('macro', 1.0); m.add_macroscopic('fuel')
    mats = openmc.Materials([m]); mats.cross_sections = str(d / 'mg.h5')
    box = openmc.model.RectangularParallelepiped(-5, 5, -5, 5, -5, 5, boundary_type='reflective')
    model = openmc.Model(geometry=openmc.Geometry([openmc.Cell(fill=m, region=-box)]), materials=mats)
    s = model.settings; s.energy_mode = 'multi-group'; s.particles = 500; s.batches = 4; s.inactive = 1
    s.source = openmc.IndependentSource(space=openmc.stats.Box((-5, -5, -5), (5, 5, 5)))
    return model

def ce_model(d):
    import openmc
    m = openmc.Material(); m.add_nuclide('U235', 2.2e-4); m.add_nuclide('H1', 6.6e-2); m.set_density('sum')
    box = openmc.model.RectangularParallelepiped(-5, 5, -5, 5, -5, 5, boundary_type='reflective')
    model = openmc.Model(geometry=openmc.Geometry([openmc.Cell(fill=m, region=-box)]), materials=openmc.Materials([m]))
    s = model.settings; s.particles = 500; s.batches = 4; s.inactive = 1
    s.source = openmc.IndependentSource(space=openmc.stats.Box((-5, -5, -5), (5, 5, 5)))
    return model

def child(order, event):
    import openmc, openmc.lib
    base = Path.cwd()
    for k, kind in enumerate(order.split('-')):
        d = base / f'{order}-{"event" if event else "history"}-{k}-{kind}'; d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        model = mg_model(d) if kind == 'mg' else ce_model(d)
        os.chdir(d)
        model.init_lib(output=False, event_based=event)
        try:
            openmc.lib.run(output=False)
            k_eff = openmc.lib.keff()
        finally:
            model.finalize_lib()
        os.chdir(base)
        print(f'run {k} {kind} done keff {k_eff[0]:.5f}', flush=True)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        child(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] == 'event'); sys.exit(0)
    res = {}
    for order in ('mg-ce', 'ce-mg', 'mg-mg', 'ce-ce'):
        for mode in ('event', 'history'):
            p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, __file__, order, mode], capture_output=True, text=True)
            res[f'{order}/{mode}'] = dict(rc=p.returncode, out=p.stdout.strip().splitlines()[-3:], err=p.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-3:])
            print(order, mode, 'rc', p.returncode, p.stdout.strip().replace('\n', ' | '), flush=True)
    json.dump(res, open('repro_v.json', 'w'), indent=1)
```

Output on develop (aa4afc41e and 3aec0edef, byte for byte the same):

```
mg-ce event rc -11 run 0 mg done keff 0.74824
mg-ce history rc 0 run 0 mg done keff 0.74824 | run 1 ce done keff 1.78385
ce-mg event rc 0 run 0 ce done keff 1.78385 | run 1 mg done keff 0.74824
ce-mg history rc 0 run 0 ce done keff 1.78385 | run 1 mg done keff 0.74824
mg-mg event rc 0 run 0 mg done keff 0.74824 | run 1 mg done keff 0.74824
mg-mg history rc 0 run 0 mg done keff 0.74824 | run 1 mg done keff 0.74824
ce-ce event rc 0 run 0 ce done keff 1.78385 | run 1 ce done keff 1.78385
ce-ce history rc 0 run 0 ce done keff 1.78385 | run 1 ce done keff 1.78385
```

`rc -11` is the child process killed by SIGSEGV. The script also writes the return codes and the last lines of each child's output to `repro_v.json`.

## Environment

- OpenMC develop at aa4afc41e (`openmc --version`: 0.16.1-dev68) and at 3aec0edef (0.16.1-dev70), each built from source with CMake: RelWithDebInfo, `-DOPENMC_ENABLE_STRICT_FP=on`, OpenMP on, MPI off, HDF5 1.10.10 (serial).
- Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64), GCC 13.3.0, Python 3.12.3 with numpy 2.5.3 and h5py 3.16.0; `OMP_NUM_THREADS=2`.
- Nuclear data: the NNDC HDF5 library of OpenMC's test suite (`cross_sections.xml` with the md5 in `tests/conftest.py`) for the continuous-energy model; the multigroup library is written by the script.

issues.title: Biased multigroup scattering when multiplicity varies with outgoing group
issues.body:
## Bug Description

I independently reproduced a multigroup transport bias in OpenMC v0.15.3 when the scattering multiplicity varies with the outgoing energy group. The bias affects track-length flux and k-effective, not only scattering tallies.

I would like to contribute a fix and upstream regression tests. I have outlined a possible correction below and would welcome feedback on the intended sampling behavior before preparing a pull request targeting `develop`.

### Expected and implemented transfer

Let:

- $C_{gh}$ be the scattering event cross section from incoming group $g$ to outgoing group $h$.
- $B_{gh}=\nu_{gh}C_{gh}$ be the corresponding neutron-production cross section, where $\nu_{gh}$ is the scattering multiplicity.
- $C_g=\sum_h C_{gh}=\Sigma_{t,g}-\Sigma_{a,g}$ and $B_g=\sum_h B_{gh}$.

The synthetic inputs below explicitly satisfy these consistency relations.

With multiplicity data, the [official library conversion](https://github.com/openmc-dev/openmc/blob/27e38e894697bb32a1dac7848d2618818b6b8daf/openmc/mgxs/library.py#L1199-L1207) supplies the nu-scatter matrix $B$. However, [the outgoing-group sampler](https://github.com/openmc-dev/openmc/blob/27e38e894697bb32a1dac7848d2618818b6b8daf/src/scattdata.cpp#L158-L170) samples $p_{gh}=B_{gh}/B_g$, and the sample methods then multiply weight by $\nu_{gh}$: [Legendre](https://github.com/openmc-dev/openmc/blob/27e38e894697bb32a1dac7848d2618818b6b8daf/src/scattdata.cpp#L366), [Histogram](https://github.com/openmc-dev/openmc/blob/27e38e894697bb32a1dac7848d2618818b6b8daf/src/scattdata.cpp#L557), and [Tabular](https://github.com/openmc-dev/openmc/blob/27e38e894697bb32a1dac7848d2618818b6b8daf/src/scattdata.cpp#L774).

Since absorption is handled before scattering, the resulting expected production matrix is

$$
B^{\mathrm{actual}}_{gh}
= C_g\frac{B_{gh}}{B_g}\nu_{gh},
$$

which generally differs from $B_{gh}$. It agrees when the multiplicity is constant across the nonzero outgoing channels of each incoming group.

### Proposed correction

Keep the existing outgoing-group probabilities and conditional angular distributions, but precompute a separate incoming-group weight multiplier:

$$
r_g=\frac{B_g}{C_g}
=\left[\sum_h\frac{p_{gh}}{\nu_{gh}}\right]^{-1}.
$$

Use this multiplier in all three sampling methods, so that

$$
C_g \cdot p_{gh} \cdot r_g = B_{gh}.
$$

For the example below, $r=(1.5,1.0)$.

Implementation considerations:

- Preserve `energy` (the normalized production distribution) and `mult` (group-to-group multiplicities), since cross-section queries and matrix reconstruction also use them.
- Initialize the separate multiplier consistently after material mixing and Legendre-to-tabular conversion.
- Skip zero-probability terms, handle empty scattering rows, and check consistency with total minus absorption rather than silently renormalizing inconsistent data.

An alternative is to maintain a separate event-based sampling distribution $C_{gh}/C_g$ and retain the group-to-group weight multiplier $\nu_{gh}$.

This correction is an expectation-level derivation. The independent reproduction attached to this report does not include a rebuilt, corrected OpenMC executable. I am willing to implement the agreed approach, add tests that fail before the fix and pass afterward, and address review feedback.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Extract the attached archive. It includes `reproduce.py`, input files, original statepoints, results, logs, and executable version output.
2. In an environment with the OpenMC Python package and executable available, run:

```bash
python reproduce.py --output results --executable openmc
python reproduce.py --output results_survival --executable openmc --survival-biasing
```

Use new output directories. No external nuclear-data library is required: the script generates synthetic two-group macroscopic data.

The fixed-source model is a homogeneous, fully reflective cube with isotropic scattering, a unit source in the high-energy group, and **no fission**. Rows are incoming groups and columns are outgoing groups. Cross sections are in $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$:

```text
Sigma_t = [1.0, 1.0]
Sigma_a = [0.6, 0.8]

C = [[0.2, 0.2],
     [0.0, 0.2]]

B = [[0.2, 0.4],
     [0.0, 0.2]]

multiplicity = [[1.0, 2.0],
                [1.0, 1.0]]
```

For the volume-integrated flux per unit external source,

$$
\left[\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma_t)-B^{T}\right]\Phi=(1,0)^{T},
$$

so the expected flux is $(1.25,0.625)$ and total absorption is $1.25$.

The implemented transfer instead gives

$$
B^{\mathrm{actual}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
2/15 & 8/15\\
0 & 1/5
\end{pmatrix},
$$

predicting the incorrect flux $(15/13,10/13)=(1.153846,0.769231)$ and absorption $17/13=1.307692$.

### Independent results

The following runs use analog absorption. Quoted uncertainties are one standard deviation.

| Case | High-energy group flux | Low-energy group flux |
|---|---:|---:|
| Correct analytical solution | 1.250000 | 0.625000 |
| Implemented-transfer prediction | 1.153846 | 0.769231 |
| OpenMC Legendre | 1.153274 ± 0.001101 | 0.768011 ± 0.001767 |
| OpenMC Histogram | 1.153138 ± 0.001129 | 0.767005 ± 0.001736 |
| OpenMC Tabular | 1.152969 ± 0.001014 | 0.766982 ± 0.001933 |

Legendre-to-tabular conversion is explicitly disabled, so these cases exercise the respective samplers. Legendre fixed-source absorption is $1.306373\pm0.001336$, consistent with the implemented-transfer prediction.

Repeating with survival biasing reproduces the same bias. Controls with all nonzero multiplicities equal to 1.0 or 1.5 agree with their analytical solutions.

The script also runs a separate eigenvalue case with fission cross sections $(0.16,0.32)$, nu-fission $(0.4,0.8)$, and $\chi=(1,0)$. Fission is included in absorption. The correct $k$ is 1.0; the implemented transfer predicts $14/13=1.076923$. The original executable gives $1.076903\pm0.000609$ with analog absorption.

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS, x86_64, running under WSL1 on Windows.
- OpenMC executable: v0.15.3, commit `27e38e894697bb32a1dac7848d2618818b6b8daf`.
- Installation: conda-forge package in Miniforge; package build `dagmc_mpi_openmpi_py313ha0fa856_102`.
- OpenMC Python package: 0.15.3; Python: 3.13.13.
- Compiler reported by the executable: GNU 14.3.0, Release build.
- Execution: one MPI process, two OpenMP threads.
- Each run: 30,000 particles per batch, 40 batches, seed 71829; eigenvalue runs discard 10 inactive batches.
- Nuclear data: synthetic macroscopic multigroup library generated by the reproducer; no continuous-energy data required.

The complete archive contains both analog and survival-biasing runs, including the constant-multiplicity controls.

issues.title: Deterministic, seed-independent dipole develops in the fission source of an exactly symmetric full-core model and biases k-eff; bank-handling channel excluded experimentally
issues.body:
**OpenMC version**: 0.15.3 release (commit 27e38e8) and a develop-branch build (commit 150f9ac0). Both produce **bit-identical** results on the attached model, and both show everything described below. Cross sections: ENDF/B-VII.1 HDF5, temperature interpolation (default 566.483 K), probability tables on. Platforms: two independent Linux builds (container GCC, HPC GCC 9.5) and an HPC cluster; identical behavior in serial (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`) and threaded.

**Summary**

For a full-core PWR model (BEAVRS rev 3.0.2 HZP, 193 assemblies, free boundaries, no symmetry BCs) that is **exactly symmetric** under the full D4 point group — verified at four independent levels (generator tables, emitted XML, pixel-wise folding of OpenMC's own `slice` plot, and the tally mesh recorded in the statepoint) — the fission source develops a **dipole tilt that is deterministic in direction** (+x, slightly −y), grows with the number of generations, and saturates at ~25–30% (E/W imbalance of the source-site weights):

| generations (inactive) | tilt_x = 100·(E−W)/(E+W) |
|---|---|
| 1 | ≈ 0 (mixed signs over 8 seeds) |
| 8 | +0.3…+2.0% (**10/10 seeds positive** over independent sweeps) |
| 30 | +6.4% |
| 120 | +16.6…+19.0% |
| 250 | +24.2% |

The ensemble mean over 20 seeds at generation 8 is **+1.58% ± 0.23%** in x and **−0.83% ± 0.16%** in y — both decisively non-zero, so the drift is *not* a realization lottery: a **seed-independent, deterministic per-generation dipole injection** exists, and the growth is fit by d(g) = D·(1−ρ^g) with D ≈ 27%, dipole/fundamental mode ratio ρ ≈ 0.991 (injection ε ≈ 2.4×10⁻³ per generation). The same mechanism biases k-eff: k rises monotonically with inactive batches (4/15/20/150 inactive → k = 1.01854 / 1.03144 / 1.03436 / 1.03546), i.e. short-inactive runs under-estimate k by up to ~150 pcm.

The tilt is present in the raw `source_bank` positions of the statepoints — it is not a tally/post-processing artifact.

**What we excluded experimentally** (each item tested, not assumed):

1. **Model asymmetry**: four independent symmetry checks (above), plus orbit-aware loading checks including burnable-absorber rod patterns (rot180 / x / y / diagonal mirrors, 96 pairs, zero mismatches).
2. **Estimator artifact**: recomputing the tilt on mirrored coordinates flips both components exactly (antisymmetric estimator).
3. **RNG stride exhaustion**: increasing `<stride>` 100× (152,917 → 15,291,700, confirmed via the statepoint attribute) leaves the tilt unchanged.
4. **Build/version**: 0.15.3 vs develop, container vs HPC — bit-identical baselines across machines.
5. **Shared-memory bank sorting**: serial runs still drift.
6. **Fission-bank slot lineage + uniform combing** (the Brown–Sutton sort feeding the combing step in `synchronize_bank`): we patched `finalize_generation` to `std::shuffle` the sorted fission bank (independent `std::mt19937_64`, seeded from `master_seed`+generation, no OpenMC stream consumed) before combing, rebuilt, and re-ran the same protocol: the tilt **survives unchanged** — 30 generations: +7.1% (baseline +6.4% on the same machine, bit-identical to the other build); 8 generations over 10 seeds: **10/10 positive, mean +1.69%** (unshuffled ensemble: +1.58% ± 0.23%). The order-preserving lineage channel is therefore *not* the carrier.
7. **Initial-source realization**: generation-1 banks are symmetric (mixed signs, 8 seeds); the direction is fixed across 10+ independent seeds and both builds.
8. **Pure slow convergence** (dominance-ratio story) *as a standalone explanation*: it cannot produce a seed-fixed direction (probability ~10⁻³–10⁻⁶ for the observed sign consistency), and the k-generation sequence of a 30-batch run shows near-white lag-1 autocorrelation (+0.33) rather than DR≈1 persistence. A slow dipole mode (ρ ≈ 0.991) is nevertheless *consistent with* the data as the **amplifier** of a deterministic injection.
9. **Model-transform invariance check**: transposing all lattice matrices of the model (the loading is D4-symmetric, so this produces the exactly mirrored physical problem) makes the tilt follow the transformation — it converts to the mirrored direction rather than staying on +x. The injection is **tied to the model and its index geometry, not to world axes** in the code.
10. **A 3×3-assembly free-boundary variant of the same fuel** shows no detectable tilt at 8 generations — consistent with the small-core dipole balance D = ε/(1−ρ_dip) being suppressed by a much smaller mode separation, though we cannot exclude that the effect requires a loosely-coupled core to become visible.

**What this looks like to us**

Everything is consistent with a **deterministic, seed-independent asymmetry entering at the transport-operator level** (magnitude ~10⁻³ per generation — far above floating-point noise, so "rule-level" rather than round-off), amplified by a slowly-decaying dipole eigenmode of the loosely-coupled core, and *locked in* by the (correlation-inducing, but unbiased) sort+combing bank cycle. We could not localize the injection point from the outside; the transport/bank source walkthrough (v0.15.3 and develop) surfaced no smoking gun, and per-generation source transition contains no shuffle by design.

**Reproducer** (~2 min)

1. Save the three attachment blocks at the bottom of this issue into an empty directory (`model.xml`, `reproduce.sh`, `shuffle-patch.diff`).
2. `export OPENMC_CROSS_SECTIONS=/path/to/endfb71/cross_sections.xml`
3. `bash reproduce.sh` — Phase A (one generation, 8 seeds) prints mixed-sign tilts; Phase B (eight generations, 5 seeds) prints the deterministic eastward drift. The script only edits `<particles>/<batches>/<inactive>/<seed>` in copies of the model.

**Impact**

Any symmetry-based validation, power-map mirror check, or entropy-only convergence gate on a loosely-coupled full-core model can silently fail: the source looks converged while carrying a 15–25% dipole, and k is biased low by up to ~150 pcm at common inactive-batch counts. We are happy to run further diagnostics — we have the model, the harness, and HPC time.

---

### `reproduce.sh`

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# reproduce.sh — MRE runner for the OpenMC upstream report (ticket 07 / PWR-IDR ticket 06).
#
# Prerequisites:
#   - openmc >= 0.15.3 on PATH (tested with 0.15.3 release, commit 27e38e8, and a
#     develop-fork build at 150f9ac0; both reproduce identically on this model)
#   - ENDF/B-VII.1 HDF5 cross sections, exported via OPENMC_CROSS_SECTIONS
#   - model.xml = the attached BEAVRS rev 3.0.2 full-core HZP model
#     (sha256 fcf2af793965ca7b857b6b9c6003eccf3cd6e8b3e63af084ae52532d912399ab)
#
# Usage:  export OPENMC_CROSS_SECTIONS=/path/to/endfb71/cross_sections.xml
#         bash reproduce.sh
#
# What it does:
#   Phase A (one generation):  100k particles, 2 batches / 1 inactive, seeds 1-8.
#     -> the final source bank is statistically symmetric (tilt signs mixed).
#   Phase B (eight generations): 100k particles, 8 batches / 4 inactive, seeds 1-5.
#     -> the final source bank is systematically tilted toward +x (east),
#        co-tilted toward -y (south), for every seed.
#   The tilt of a source bank is 100*(E-W)/(E+W) over the fission-site weights,
#   printed by the embedded python below.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

run_case () {  # $1=tag  $2=particles  $3=batches  $4=inactive  $5=seed
  cp model.xml "model-$1.xml"
  sed -i "s|<particles>1000</particles>|<particles>$2</particles>|; s|<batches>120</batches>|<batches>$3</batches>|; s|<inactive>20</inactive>|<inactive>$4</inactive>|; s|<seed>20261003</seed>|<seed>$5</seed>|" "model-$1.xml"
  rm -f "statepoint.$3.h5" summary.h5
  OMP_NUM_THREADS="${OMP_NUM_THREADS:-4}" openmc "model-$1.xml" >/dev/null 2>&1
  python3 - "statepoint.$3.h5" <<'PYEOF'
import sys
import h5py
import numpy as np
sp = sys.argv[1]
f = h5py.File(sp, 'r')
r = f['source_bank']['r'][()]
w = f['source_bank']['wgt'][()]
x, y = r['x'].astype(float), r['y'].astype(float)
Ew, Ww = w[x > 0].sum(), w[x < 0].sum()
Nw, Sw = w[y > 0].sum(), w[y < 0].sum()
print('%s tilt_x=%+.3f%% tilt_y=%+.3f%% (n=%d)'
      % (sp, 100 * (Ew - Ww) / (Ew + Ww), 100 * (Nw - Sw) / (Nw + Sw), len(x)))
f.close()
PYEOF
  rm -f "model-$1.xml"
}

echo "== Phase A: one fission generation (expect mixed signs) =="
for s in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do run_case "1g-s$s" 100000 2 1 "$s"; done
echo "== Phase B: eight generations (expect all tilted +x / -y) =="
for s in 1 2 3 4 5; do run_case "8g-s$s" 100000 8 4 "$s"; done
echo "REPRO_DONE"
```

### `shuffle-patch.diff` — E3 bank-shuffle experiment (applied on top of 150f9ac0; tilt survives, lineage channel excluded)

```diff
E3 shuffle patch (applied to the develop-fork tree, commit 150f9ac0; the same
call site exists in v0.15.3 as sort_fission_bank in src/bank.cpp + the
finalize_generation block in src/simulation.cpp). Exact applied change:

--- a/src/simulation.cpp
+++ b/src/simulation.cpp
@@ (includes)
 #include <algorithm>
 #include <cmath>
+#include <random>
 #include <numeric>
@@ (finalize_generation, inside the eigenvalue/MONTE_CARLO block)
     sort_bank(simulation::fission_bank, true);
+
+    // E3 PATCH: randomly shuffle the sorted fission bank before combing,
+    // to break the parent-id slot lineage. Independent RNG
+    // (std::mt19937_64, seeded from master_seed + generation); consumes
+    // no OpenMC random-number stream.
+    {
+      extern int64_t master_seed;
+      std::mt19937_64 e3_rng(
+          static_cast<uint64_t>(master_seed) * 1000003ULL +
+          static_cast<uint64_t>(overall_generation()));
+      std::shuffle(simulation::fission_bank.data(),
+          simulation::fission_bank.data() + simulation::fission_bank.size(),
+          e3_rng);
+    }
 
     // Distribute fission bank across processors evenly
     synchronize_bank();

Result: the deterministic source tilt is unchanged (30 generations:
+7.09% vs +6.44% baseline on the same machine/protocol; 8 generations over
10 seeds: 10/10 positive, mean +1.69% vs +1.58% ± 0.23% unshuffled).
```

issues.title: feat(blender): put unkeyed bones at rest when Apply animation assigns a clip
issues.body:
## Why

Apply animation (#522) copies a returned clip onto the user's own rig. Bones that the clip does not key, such as a static Root above Hips, keep whatever pose the rig already had, so the clip can play from a displaced or rotated pose. On the returned rig those bones are at rest. Review finding: https://github.com/scenario-labs/blender-plugin/pull/522#discussion_r4307048826

## Proposal

When Apply animation assigns the first clip, put the destination bones that exist in the returned rig but are not keyed by any copied clip back to rest (identity location, rotation and scale). Record their previous pose so rollback and Undo restore it exactly. Leave bones that the returned rig does not have untouched.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A posed, unkeyed Root is at rest after Apply animation, and its pose is restored after a failed application and after Undo.
- [ ] Bones absent from the returned rig keep their pose.
- [ ] Installed tests on Blender 5.0, 5.1 and 5.2.

issues.title: ci(tests): track coverage on main and report and gate it in pull requests
issues.body:
## Problem

CI measures unit-test statement coverage on every run (`unit (3.11)` and `unit (3.13)`), but
nothing tracks it: there is no minimum, the reports expire after 14 days, and no pull request
shows how it moved the figure. A drop goes unnoticed unless someone opens the artifact.

The figure also mixes in code the unit suite can never reach. On main (14fb642), the unit run
measures 88.0% of `scenario/core` and `scenario/mcp`:

| Scope | Statements | Covered |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `scenario/core` | 18,386 | 95.9% |
| `scenario/mcp`, without the modules below | 700 | 96.0% |
| `mcp/tools_blender.py`, `mcp/tools_scenario.py` (import `bpy`) | 1,694 | 0% |
| `mcp/stdio_shim.py` (runs as a subprocess) | 43 | 0% |

`scenario/blender`, `scenario/__init__.py` and `scenario/prefs.py` are not measured at all; only
the headless Blender suite exercises them.

## Scope

1. Keep main's coverage for each commit beyond the 14-day artifact and show the trend.
2. On pull requests, report total and changed-line coverage against main in the job summary or
   a comment, fork-safe: read-only token, no secret.
3. Gate regressions: a `fail_under` in `pyproject.toml` just below the baseline, computed
   without the Blender-only modules so it reflects what unit tests can reach, raised as
   coverage grows.
4. Decide whether to measure Blender-side code by running coverage.py inside the headless suite
   (`tools/test_blender.py`) and combining it with the unit data. A separate issue is fine if it
   is large.

Prefer an in-repo approach (main's report kept as the baseline, diffed in pull requests) over an
external service such as Codecov: no account or upload token, and fork pull requests keep
working with a read-only token. Any new tool needs a pinned development dependency.

## Acceptance

- A pull request shows its total and changed-line coverage versus main without opening an
  artifact.
- Main's coverage history is visible beyond 14 days.
- A pull request that drops coverage below the gate fails `ci-ok`.
- `docs/development/validation.md` describes the tracking, the gate and the measured scope.

issues.title: feat(schema): surface the background-removal hint that model inputs declare with backgroundBehavior
issues.body:
## What

Some model inputs declare `backgroundBehavior`. For example, the reference image of Tripo 3.1 image-to-3D declares `"transparent"`, and several image and video models declare `"opaque"`. The Scenario web app uses this flag to suggest removing the background before generating. SDK 2.4.0 types the field as `background_behavior: "opaque" | "transparent"`.

The extension ignores the flag. It appears only in test fixtures (`tests/fixtures/models/model_tripo-v3-1-image-to-3d.json`), never in `scenario/core/schema/`. So the native panels and the local MCP `render_form` never tell an artist or an agent that an image-to-3D reference works best with a transparent background.

## Evidence

- Internal image-to-3D tests compared the same Tripo 3.1 generation with and without background removal on the reference image. The result changed noticeably. The tests also found that agents never see the recommendation through the hosted MCP's schema.
- Image-to-3D is one of the extension's main lanes, and a reference image dropped from the scene or the file browser often has an opaque background.

## Proposal (needs a product decision)

1. Parse `backgroundBehavior` into the parameter spec.
2. When an image input declares `"transparent"` and the chosen image has no alpha channel, show a one-line hint in the native panel. Add the same hint to the field's description in the local MCP form.
3. Optional: offer the existing background-removal tool model as a one-click step. This step spends credits, so it needs its own price check and a person's yes before it is built.

Steps 1 and 2 are free and local. Step 3 touches spending and UX.

Handled by the plugin-engineer routine. Opening this as an issue rather than a PR because the UX needs a person's decision.

issues.title: async_update_interfaces does not report whether the requested interfaces were bound
issues.body:
## Problem

`Zeroconf.async_update_interfaces` is best-effort and returns `None`, so a caller cannot tell whether the requested configuration was applied.

Two failure paths are logged and swallowed:

- A listen socket rebuild that fails, for example switching an IPv4 instance to `IPVersion.All` on a host that cannot open a dual-stack `AF_INET6` socket. The engine logs `Skipping interface update; listen socket rebuild failed` and returns `False`.
- A requested interface that fails to bind. The engine logs `Interface ... not added` once and carries on.

In both cases `Zeroconf.async_update_interfaces` still commits the requested `interfaces` and `ip_version` as the retained configuration, and returns normally.

## Where

- [Engine rebuild failure](https://github.com/python-zeroconf/python-zeroconf/blob/4b6bd74a84d7f3382d5475a27ff7fd6ed0f4ceaf/src/zeroconf/_engine.py#L179-L188) returns `False`, the same value as "nothing was added".
- [`_async_add_interface`](https://github.com/python-zeroconf/python-zeroconf/blob/4b6bd74a84d7f3382d5475a27ff7fd6ed0f4ceaf/src/zeroconf/_engine.py#L238-L256) returns `False` for an interface that did not come up.
- [`Zeroconf.async_update_interfaces`](https://github.com/python-zeroconf/python-zeroconf/blob/4b6bd74a84d7f3382d5475a27ff7fd6ed0f4ceaf/src/zeroconf/_core.py#L414-L457) uses the engine's result only to decide whether to re-announce.

## Why it matters

A caller that asks for dual-stack and cannot get it has no signal to fall back to `IPVersion.V4Only`, or to retry later. It also cannot log an accurate outcome: a caller that logs "reconciled with IPVersion.All" after a swallowed rebuild failure is wrong.

In esphome/device-builder#2864 this meant a runtime IPv4-only fallback could not be implemented, because the failure it would react to never surfaces.

## Suggested fix

Report the outcome from the public method. Options:

- Return whether the desired interface set fully bound, or the list of interfaces that were skipped.
- Raise when the address family rebuild fails, since in that case none of the requested change was applied.

Either keeps the best-effort behaviour for per-interface failures while letting callers react.

issues.title: feat(dashboard): show existing explicit and Dream operation outcomes across artifact pages
issues.body:
## Feature description

Implementation sub-issue of #2130: present available explicit-operation and Dream evidence on applicable Artifact pages, including Skill, Prompt and Handoff, and the explicit/Dream paths of other families.

Use existing operation records and exact result references where available. Clearly state when asynchronous processing status is not applicable or when an outcome is unavailable.

## Problem and proposed solution

Source-consumption positions cannot explain every Artifact path. A Skill derivation or Experience refinement can have a retained Dream run, while a synchronous generation path may have no retained asynchronous lifecycle. Prompt configuration/availability badges describe a different fact from an operation's outcome.

Inventory each supported path and adapt its existing read API or record into the parent's compact status section and details presentation. Reuse existing scoped Dream list/get reads for supported operations; inspect any other path's actual evidence before promising an outcome. Do not create new operation history to fill missing fields.

A Dream success can produce a pending Candidate rather than publish an Artifact. The view must preserve that distinction and use exact references for any result it displays.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Complete the family/path coverage matrix for explicit generation, supported Dream operations and Handoff outcomes. Record which paths have retained operation evidence, which have genuinely associated local observations, and where status is unavailable or inapplicable.
- [ ] Render bilingual status/details on applicable pages using bounded existing queries or links to existing records. Clearly distinguish a selected Artifact's exact operation/result from a separately labeled Scope-level recent operation.
- [ ] Associate evidence using the authorized Scope, actual operation and available exact references. Never label an unrelated latest Dream run as the selected Artifact's current status.
- [ ] Distinguish accepted/queued/running/terminal operation state, Candidate creation, Artifact publication and an explicitly known no-change outcome. Successful generation or Candidate creation must not be labeled as publication.
- [ ] Preserve historical outcomes and timestamps without treating an earlier failure as an unresolved current failure after later success. Local observations include coverage/freshness; after restart, unavailable local history stays unavailable.
- [ ] For paths without an asynchronous lifecycle, mark that dimension not applicable. Where a lifecycle/result may exist but cannot be inspected, report unavailable. Do not fabricate operation identities or introduce a universal state machine.
- [ ] Preserve selected-Scope and exact-record authorization. Use bounded pagination/filtering instead of scanning complete run history; failures in this section must not prevent independent Artifact reads. Any necessary public contract extension follows the RFC/generated OpenAPI workflow.
- [ ] Inspection must remain passive: no generation, readiness probes, approval, retry, cancel, resume, budget reset or business/processing-state writes.
- [ ] Verify queued/active/terminal Dream records, Candidate-only success, known no-change results, historical failure followed by success, absent/unobservable evidence, unrelated exact references, Scope isolation and partial read failure. Exercise the Dashboard behavior with controlled records rather than production model calls.
- [ ] Combine this slice with #2308 (Topic Memory) and #2309 (Source consumption) to verify #2130's full cross-page acceptance. Document each supported/unavailable/inapplicable path and interpretation in both locales.

## Alternatives considered

Applying Source cursors to explicit/Dream operations invents a lifecycle. Treating every successful Dream as publication hides pending review. Adding a new task ledger or complete history solely for the Dashboard expands the parent issue beyond its existing-evidence contract.

## Additional context

Baseline: master `bf2ac1fcd9223af7bbab97f8e8e39a269b07fee3`, checked on 2026-10-30.

- [Dream run and Candidate-reference models](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/bf2ac1fcd9223af7bbab97f8e8e39a269b07fee3/src/powercontext/builtin/dream/models.py)
- [Existing scoped Dream reads](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/bf2ac1fcd9223af7bbab97f8e8e39a269b07fee3/src/powercontext/builtin/dream/application.py)
- [Public API contract, including Dream list/get](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/bf2ac1fcd9223af7bbab97f8e8e39a269b07fee3/openapi/powercontext.yaml)
- [Current Prompt page](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/bf2ac1fcd9223af7bbab97f8e8e39a269b07fee3/src/powercontext/server/dashboard/templates/prompts.html)
- [Current Handoff page](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/bf2ac1fcd9223af7bbab97f8e8e39a269b07fee3/src/powercontext/server/dashboard/templates/handoff.html)

Duplicate check: all 86 open issues and the changed-file lists of all 33 open PRs were checked. No open equivalent Dashboard implementation issue/PR was found. #2130 is the parent; #1984 covers broader outcome explanations and #2105 targets Desktop. #2270 proposes a durable Work Ledger but does not implement these Dashboard pages and is not required to display existing records. #2244 changes authorization imports only.

Coordinate read-boundary/presentation conventions with #2308 and #2309. Keep new recovery policy with #2128, diagnostic export outside this issue, and operation behavior at its owning service. Closing this slice can close #2130 only after the other slices and the parent's complete acceptance criteria are verified.

issues.title: [Previous Contributors Response Needed] Transition python-zeroconf to the Apache-2.0 License
issues.body:
## Why `python-zeroconf` sits under a long list of Python projects. #1123 asked for a permissive license in 2023, and the same request has reached me many times since, mostly in private conversations with developers in the Matter and smart home space. When #1123 was raised I discussed it with jstasiak, the only other active maintainer at the time, and [they agreed](https://github.com/python-zeroconf/python-zeroconf/issues/1123#issuecomment-1411451210) a permissive license would be fine for their contributions; this issue proposes Apache 2.0, one of the two licenses that request named. The LGPL's relinking requirement is deliberate: it guarantees users can swap in their own build of the library. That is easy for ordinary Python deployments and hard for frozen binaries and other sealed distributions (#276, #1363 and #1385 are all people shipping the library inside frozen executables, none of whom raised the license), so projects in those settings avoid the dependency or go without. In practice it mostly gets lumped into a blanket no-LGPL policy rather than weighed on its own, and projects only notice when it becomes a problem, so little of this is public; an example is OpenVoiceOS's license checks flagging the dependency (OpenVoiceOS/ovos-core#546). As maintainer, my call is that this protection is not worth the users it costs. The change has a price too: some contributors declined, and all of their surviving expression had to be removed and replaced (tracked below, down to a disclosed set of single-statement lines any implementation would share). This is the consent-based approach LLVM used, with declined contributions removed rather than relicensed; nothing already released changes license. To be clear about what this is not (since it was asked below): I am self-employed, no company employs me or directs my work, all my time on this project is volunteer time given freely with as few strings attached as possible, and I do not profit from it. No company asked me for this, I personally deliberately accept no sponsorships of any kind to avoid even a potential misalignment (I do not have GitHub Sponsors enabled), and any legal review gets paid out of my own pocket. Nobody wants to be the person asking everyone for relicensing consent; I just happen to be the one maintaining the project now. We likely will keep LGPL-2.1-or-later as an OR option for strict GPL-2.0-only compatibility. It is unlikely to be needed, but part of this is to avoid licensing discussions which take maintainer time, and friction wherever possible. Keeping the LGPL option needs no new consent, since those grants already exist; the consent being collected here is what enables the Apache option, and that is the same work either way. ## The ask We plan to migrate python-zeroconf from LGPL-2.1-or-later to [Apache 2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0). To do this we need every contributor's permission to relicense their contributions. If you are a contributor, please respond to this issue with something along the lines of: > I consent to my contributions to the python-zeroconf repository being relicensed under Apache 2.0 in place of the current LGPL license. (Future contributions arrive under both Apache 2.0 and LGPL-2.1-or-later via the notice on every pull request; we may keep the LGPL as an OR option so GPL-2.0-only projects can keep using the library. No ongoing obligation is created by consenting here.) Consent covers your commits authored on or before the date of your comment; later contributions are covered by the license notice posted on every pull request, and blame will be re-verified against consent dates before any switch. Declining is a normal option and is honored the way it has been so far: your surviving contributions are removed and replaced, nothing more. Each verified consent is also recorded in a ledger committed to the repository (username, commit emails, comment link, date), so the record cannot drift after the fact. Feel free to turn off notifications afterwards. ## pyzeroconf heritage python-zeroconf exists thanks to pyzeroconf, created by Paul Scott-Murphy in 2003 and carried forward by William McBrine. This project would not be here without their work, and their names will stay in the project's history and acknowledgements regardless of the license. An initial `git blame` line audit understated what survives from that era; blame credits whoever moved code in the 2021 package split. An expanded audit with move and copy detection, run after @wmcbrine's comment below, found that a meaningful amount of Paul's 2009 expression was still in the tree, mostly docstrings, so he was added to the table. After both declined, all of that expression was removed and replaced through successive rounds of progressively stronger audits (blame, move aware blame, word n-grams, character level, fuzzy paraphrase, block level, AST structure, exact whole unit, arrangement comparison, and an adversarial re-audit); the removal history below lists every round. The original line by line findings are preserved in the expanded audit sections as a historical record. issues.title: Link-local AAAA records stay unscoped on a dual-stack host: the scoped IPv6 copy is dropped as a duplicate of the IPv4 one (follow-up to #1567)
issues.body:
#1764 made `parsed_scoped_addresses()` prefer a scoped copy of an AAAA record when an unscoped one is also cached, and left "the IPv4-only-arrival case" for a follow-up. I couldn't find an issue for that follow-up, so here it is with measurements. In short: on a dual-stack host the scoped copy usually never reaches the cache, so #1764 has nothing to prefer. Disabling packet duplicate suppression is enough for 0.151.5 to return `fe80::…%<idx>`.

## Setup

- **Querier:** Linux 6.12, 32-bit ARM (armv7l), Python 3.14. One wired interface (index 2) with IPv4, a link-local address, and global and ULA IPv6 addresses (SLAAC, with temporary addresses). `AsyncZeroconf(ip_version=IPVersion.All)`, default interfaces.
- **Peers:** embedded devices on the same link. Each answers with its A record and three AAAA records (link-local, global, ULA) in one message, over both IPv4 and IPv6.
- **Version:** 0.151.5, and master at f0c27b38 (2026-10-01), whose `src/zeroconf` is identical to 0.151.5. Both were run as pure Python so `AsyncListener._process_datagram_at_time` could be wrapped. For every response carrying a peer's link-local AAAA, the wrapper logged which socket it arrived on, the sender's address, and the scope zeroconf would give it. It logged before the duplicate check runs.
- **Control:** a plain IPv6 UDP socket on 5353, joined to ff02::fb on interface 2, sent an AAAA query. All 18 peers answered by multicast from their `fe80::` address, and `recvfrom` gave scope 2 for every one. The peers do their part, and the kernel supplies the scope.

## Results

**One-shot lookups:** `AddressResolver(host).async_request(zc, 3000)`, a fresh instance each time, 10 rounds over 3 peers (0.151.5).

| Measurement | 0.151.5 |
|---|---|
| Lookups where `parsed_scoped_addresses()` gave a usable link-local scope | 0 / 30 |
| IPv6 respond socket bound to a global address, not link-local | 30 / 30 |
| First copy of the link-local AAAA in an IPv4 packet (scope `None`) | 14 |
| First copy by unicast IPv6 from the peer's global address (scope 0) | 16 |
| A scoped copy (from the peer's `fe80::`, scope 2) received at all | 1 |
| ...that ended up in the cache | 0 |

In that one lookup, the IPv4 copy arrived on the `::` listen socket from v4-mapped `::ffff:192.0.2.x` (scope 0) at 571 ms. The IPv6 copy from the peer's `fe80::` address (scope 2) followed at 573 ms. The cache ended with only the scope-0 and `None` entries.

**Browsing:** an `AsyncServiceBrowser` for the peers' service type, with the cache read every 10 s.

- **Unmodified (0.151.5, 300 s):** the link-local addresses stayed unscoped throughout.
- **0.151.5 with `_DUPLICATE_PACKET_SUPPRESSION_INTERVAL = 0`, otherwise unchanged:** the same pair (v4-mapped first, `fe80::` 4 ms later) arrived at 202 s for all three peers. From then on the cache held a scope-2 entry for each, and `parsed_scoped_addresses()` returned `fe80::…%2` for all three.

**Duplicate drops on master:** a 300 s browse with debug logging logged 43 "Ignoring duplicate message" lines for packets from the peers' `fe80::` addresses. Those are the only copies that carry a scope. It also logged 183 for v4-mapped senders. All were on the `::` socket.

## Why: four ways the scope is lost

1. **Duplicate suppression ignores the sender.** The IPv6 listen socket is bound to `::` with `IPV6_V6ONLY` off, so it receives both IPv4 and IPv6 multicast. A peer's IPv4 and IPv6 announcements are byte-identical, and the IPv4 copy usually arrives first. The listener's duplicate checks compare payload bytes only: both the last-packet check and the `_recent_packets` cache from #1750. So the IPv6 copy, the only one that carries a scope, is dropped. #1750 keeps that state per listener "so a duplicate seen on one interface does not suppress" a packet arriving on another. But with the dual-stack `::` socket, the IPv4 and IPv6 sides of one interface share a listener. #1764 can't help, because the scoped record never reaches the cache.
2. **The IPv4 copy is scoped from its sender.** On the `::` socket it arrives as `::ffff:a.b.c.d` with scope 0. That gives a cache entry with scope 0, which is no more usable than one with none.
3. **The first answer comes over IPv4, unicast.** The first query is QU, so the peer answers by unicast to the query's source address, and an IPv4 answer carries the AAAA records too. It arrives on the IPv4 respond socket, so it has no scope, although that socket belongs to one interface.
4. **The IPv6 respond socket is bound to a global address.** zeroconf binds one IPv6 respond socket per interface, to one of the interface's addresses. Here it was always a global one (which one varied between runs), never the link-local. So a QU answer over IPv6 comes from the peer's global address, and the scope taken from that sender is 0.

## The RFCs

- **RFC 6762 §6.2:** a responder "MUST include all addresses that are valid on the interface on which it is sending the message". The RFC's example is a link-local plus a routable address, "so that queriers receive both and can make their own choice", and it says this "allows a querier that only has an IPv6 link-local address to connect to the link-local address". The same section says a responder SHOULD include the other address type in the additional section, so that "all a device's addresses are delivered atomically in a single message". An AAAA record arriving in an IPv4 packet (cases 1 to 3) is therefore normal, conformant behaviour, not an edge case.
- **RFC 6762 §14:** addresses in responses "MUST be valid for use on the interface on which the response is being sent", and a host needs "network programming APIs that allow applications ... to discover on what interface a Multicast DNS response was received". So a link-local address in a response belongs to the interface the response arrived on. For the respond sockets that interface is known, since each is bound to one. The shared `::` listen socket serves every interface, so there it isn't known. Either way, the sender's sockaddr only gives the interface when the sender happens to be link-local.
- **RFC 6762 §5.4:** the first questions are QU, and "a responder SHOULD usually respond with a unicast packet directed back to the querier". That is why the first answer arrives unicast, on whichever family and source address the query went out from (cases 3 and 4).
- **RFC 6762 §20:** a dual-stack host "acts like a multihomed host, with one connection to the logical 'IPv4 Ethernet segment', and a connection to the logical 'IPv6 Ethernet segment'". On that view an IPv4 and an IPv6 copy of the same answer are two separate arrivals, not a duplicate packet (case 1).
- **RFC 4007 §6 and §11.2:** a non-global address needs a zone index, and zone 0 or no zone means the default zone. Linux has no default zone for link-local addresses, so connecting to `fe80::…` or `fe80::…%0` fails with `EINVAL`. A cache entry with scope 0 is as unusable as one with none.

## Possible fixes

Roughly from smallest to largest:

- **Key duplicate suppression on the scope the packet's records would get** (`addrs[3]`, 0 otherwise), so the scoped IPv6 copy of an answer isn't dropped behind the unscoped IPv4 one (case 1). This looks like the change that would matter most in practice. The control above shows it's enough for #1764 to work whenever a peer multicasts over IPv6. PR #1926 does this.
- **Don't scope records from a v4-mapped sender** (case 2). Those packets are IPv4, and scope 0 means "unknown".
- **Bind the per-interface IPv6 respond socket to the interface's link-local address** (case 4). QU answers over IPv6 then come from the peer's link-local address, with the right scope.
- **Scope link-local AAAA records from the receiving interface**, IPv4 packets included (case 3), as RFC 6762 §14 describes. The draft #1568 ("Use per-interface per-protocol sockets") does this: one socket per interface and per address family, each listener stamping its interface index on what it receives, and IPv6 bound to link-local. That would also cover cases 1, 2 and 4. The alternative #1567 mentions is `IP_PKTINFO`/`IPV6_RECVPKTINFO` with `recvmsg`.

Our workaround in the meantime is to derive the scope ourselves: the interface whose IPv4 subnet or IPv6 prefix contains one of the peer's other addresses.

We'd be glad to help further, including running any patched build (#1568 rebased, for instance) against the same peers with the same measurements.
